To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the Hilton et al. study is a key evidence supporting current iatrogenic risk reduction measures; 2) transgenic mice expressing PrP 129Met are useful for bioassay of vCJD lymphoid tissue; 3) vCJD prionic infectivity in lymphoreticular tissue is reduced by formalin‐fixation; 4) the Hilton et all. study should continue to be interpreted as evidence of vCJD prevalence pending the outcome of other
(i) vCJD prionic infectivity is present in lymphoreticular tissue, including appendix and spleen, but not in brain, and (ii) fixation with formalin destroys infectivity in lymphoreticular tissues.

we found that formalin fixation reduced the infectivity of human vCJD brain prions by 1.5 log10 ID50 units, and that we were unable to detect vCJD prionic infectivity in two formalin‐fixed vCJD appendix specimens that were previously reported to be vCJD‐infected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of fixation and the bioassay of vCJD lymphoid tissue.
the effects of fixation and the bioassay of lymphoreticular vCID prions.
the effects of fixation of lymphoreticular and brain vCJD priones and their bioassay in transgenic mice expressing either human PrP 29M (HuPrP-Tg) or human PrP 219M (HuPrPTg).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Hilton et al. (2004) study has not been confirmed and that it should not be used as the basis for public health policy.
the Hilton et al prevalence study is inconclusive and should be repeated on a larger scale with the use of a more sensitive detection assay.
there is no evidence of a significant prevalence of vCjd in any of the tissues examined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of fixation and the lack of a gold standard test for human prion diseases are still limiting the progress of research in this area.
we are still unable to confirm the Hilton study results using our transgenic mouse bioassay system.
we have shown that formalin fixation does not reduce infectivity in the brain of vCJD patients but does in the spleen.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the effects of fixation are not uniform across all tissues, and that the effects of formalin‐fixation on prion titres are likely to be dependent on the type of prion strain and the tissue being fixed.
we have demonstrated that fixation of lymphoreticular tissue can have a profound impact on the infectivity of vCJD.
fixation of vCJD tissue in formalin does not appear to destroy the infectivity of the vCJD prione.
